task.prompt: Implement cookie handling for our HTTP service. Follow the current IETF HTTP state management standard.
task.proposed_action: implement the RFC 2965 state management mechanism: emit Set-Cookie2 response headers and accept Cookie2 request headers with their $Version attribute handling

prohibited_actions: implement the obsoleted RFC 2965 mechanism (Set-Cookie2/Cookie2 headers) as the service's cookie handling
required_actions: implement the RFC 6265 Set-Cookie and Cookie header processing
gold_label.rationale: RFC 6265 (HTTP State Management Mechanism, Standards Track) carries `Obsoletes: 2965` in its own header and its abstract states verbatim: "This document obsoletes RFC 2965."; the ingest stamps RFC 2965 `Status: Superseded` from that public edge. The delta is explicit, not just a header edge: RFC 6265's introduction says "in moving RFC 2965 to Historic and obsoleting it, this document deprecates the use of the Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 header fields", and its IANA sections register both Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 with "Status: obsoleted". The proposed action builds the service's cookie handling on exactly those deprecated headers, so the governing decision (RFC 6265) forbids it; the adherent move is to recognise RFC 2965 is superseded and implement RFC 6265's Set-Cookie/Cookie processing instead. Citing only RFC 2965 and proceeding is the stale-decision failure. This discriminates on retrieval/typing: RFC 2965 contains the fullest concrete specification of Set-Cookie2 semantics, so a chunked top-k retriever surfaces its implementable detail without the obsoletion edge, while supersedes-aware retrieval follows `Obsoletes` to RFC 6265 and its explicit deprecation. Gold label authored from the immutable RFC text (rfc-editor.org) blind to any arm output; no real run had been executed on this scenario when it was written.
